articles.title: _TimeOut_ Names the World's 28 'Coolest' Streets
articles.intro: Explore TimeOut's list of the world's 28 coolest streets, featuring hotspots for food, art, and culture in cities across the globe.

sentences.text: What makes a part of a city "cool"?
Is it clubs?
Cafes?
Unique local shops?
_TimeOut_ has released its list of the world's 28 "coolest" streets for 2026.
And according to the magazine, a "cool" street is a place where people "want to spend their time right now."
That means these streets are "home to some of the very best places to eat, drink, dance, shop and hang out" in each city.
The magazine asked its editors and local experts for their ideas, and they decided that the coolest street in the world for 2026 is Song Wat Road in Bangkok, Thailand.
This {{prn:1,200-meter-long|one thousand and two hundred meter long}} street was once an important trade hub between Bangkok's Chinatown and the Chao Phraya River.
But these days, its old brick warehouses are full of restaurants, colorful street art, independent fashion stores and more!
In second place is London's Golborne Road.
It's known for its mix of Portuguese, Moroccan and Middle Eastern restaurants, as well as bars, cafes and vintage clothing shops.
In third place is Fernández de Enciso in Buenos Aires, Argentina.
This street has lots of cafes and restaurants where visitors can sit outside and eat under the trees.
Nearby Plaza Arenales is also a popular meeting place, where there are often events and live music.
Four of _TimeOut'_s 10 coolest streets are in Asia, with Singapore's Neil Road at number five, Hong Kong's Upper Lascar Row at number seven, and Beach Street in George Town, Malaysia, at number nine.
There are also two Japanese streets on the list.
Sanjo-dori in Kyoto is in 13th place.
It's known for its old red-brick buildings, many of which are now cafes, galleries and shops.
Oyafuko Street in Fukuoka is number 25.
_TimeOut_ said its list shows the "variety of street life" around the world.

articles.title: Japan Plans to Make It Easier to Become a Teacher
articles.intro: This lesson covers Japan's plan to ease requirements for becoming a teacher in response to a nationwide shortage of teaching staff.

sentences.text: Japan is planning to make it easier for working adults, or students who majored in another subject, to switch to a career in teaching.
A government education panel released a proposal on November 17 to make teaching licenses easier to get.
The goal is to encourage more people to enter a profession that is struggling to find enough staff.
One change would make it easier for university students to qualify.
At the moment, those preparing to teach in elementary, junior high or high schools must earn 59 credits in teaching-related subjects.
Under the new plan, this would fall to 36 or 37 credits.
Students would still need another 20 credits, but these could come from subjects they are already studying for their degree.
This would make it easier for students from different fields to become teachers.
The proposal would also include a one-year graduate course for working adults who hold a university degree or higher.
They would learn about teaching and spend time working in schools, where they would also receive compensation.
The plan comes as schools across Japan struggle to find enough workers.
According to an education ministry survey, more than 2,800 public schools in Japan started the 2025 academic year without enough teachers.
And fewer people are choosing teaching jobs.
In 2025, there were just 2.9 people applying for every teaching job, down from 3.2 a year earlier.
That was the lowest number on record.
The panel plans to finalize its recommendations by the end of 2026, with changes to the law expected to be proposed in 2027.

articles.title: Okinawa Celebrates Restoration of Shuri Castle
articles.intro: Learn about the restoration of Shuri Castle in Okinawa, its history, cultural significance, and impact after a devastating fire.

sentences.text: Officials and residents in Okinawa celebrated the restoration of Shuri Castle's main hall on November 22, seven years after it was destroyed in a fire.
The building, famous for its deep red color and dragon decorations, is an important symbol of Okinawa's cultural heritage.
The fire broke out on October 31, 2019 during a festival at the castle complex in Naha, Okinawa's capital.
Firefighters struggled for nearly 12 hours to contain the blaze as it spread in strong winds.
The fire destroyed the main hall, two halls next to it and four nearby structures, while two other structures were heavily damaged.
Investigators could not determine the cause but considered an electrical fault the likeliest explanation.
"The fire was a tremendous shock to the Okinawan people," Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said at the restoration ceremony.
Shuri Castle dates back to the Ryukyu Kingdom, which ruled Okinawa for about 450 years until Japan took control in 1879.
The castle also represents Okinawa's recovery from World War II.
It was destroyed during the Battle of Okinawa in 1945, which killed about 200,000 people, including many civilians.
The castle was largely rebuilt in 1992, but work on some sections was still underway when the 2019 fire occurred.
For the latest restoration, experts used historical documents and new research to make the main hall more closely resemble the original building.
They even recreated its distinctive deep red color using a pigment made partly from iron bacteria found in northern Okinawa.
The main hall reopened to the public on November 23, while restoration of other buildings will continue in stages.
Experts say completing the entire castle could take more than a decade.
Shuri Castle is a major tourist attraction, and its restoration is expected to boost Okinawa's economy.
Koja, who took office in September, has promised to double the island's per capita income and tourism revenue within a decade and make it more attractive to young people.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Reinstated as Nvidia CEO
articles.intro: This lesson covers Jensen Huang’s resignation and swift return as Nvidia CEO amid scandals, board decisions, political intervention, and market impact.

sentences.text: Jensen Huang has made an unlikely comeback as CEO of Nvidia just 11 days after resigning from the US chipmaker and six days after its board rejected his offer to return.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia, stepped down on November 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of working as a spy for Beijing.
Nvidia's board had initially expressed confidence in Huang's leadership while launching an investigation into the allegations.
However, pressure compounded after reports emerged of another alleged affair, this time with an Nvidia employee who reported directly to him.
The day after Huang's resignation, supporters launched an online petition calling for his reinstatement.
It gained support from many current and former Nvidia employees, investors and prominent tech industry figures, including Elon Musk.
On November 17, Huang acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life and said he would be "honored" to return as CEO if the board believed it was in the company's best interests.
However, the board firmly rejected the idea.
President Donald Trump continued lobbying for Huang's return, both publicly and behind the scenes.
Trump worried that Huang's departure was hurting the stock market and could put the US behind China in the race for technological dominance.
"I'm doing it for the country," Trump told _CNBC_.
On November 23, Nvidia's board reversed its decision, announcing that Huang would return as CEO with immediate effect.
Trump took credit for the sudden reversal, saying: "The board decided to do what we wanted them to do."
Nvidia said it had received input from senior US government officials and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
Several Democratic politicians have criticized Trump's intervention, arguing that economic interests were being put ahead of national security.
Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday following the announcement, helping the broader US stock market recover from a week of heavy losses.
Meanwhile, Huang expressed gratitude for the support he had received.
"I am going to be a better CEO the second time around," he said.
However, Huang still faces several investigations concerning the affair and the suspected transfer of Nvidia's advanced computer chips to China.

articles.title: Study Shows Where in Lungs Vapes' Toxic Metals Go
articles.intro: Explore research on how toxic metals from vaping accumulate in different parts of the lungs and their potential health risks.

sentences.text: According to the World Health Organization, more than 100 million people around the world — including at least 15 million children — use e-cigarettes.
E-cigarettes and vaping are often marketed as a safer alternative to cigarettes.
However, not only do they still contain addictive nicotine, but research has found that they may leave toxic metals in users' lungs.
Some of these metals are in the liquid used to give e-cigarettes their flavor, but some also come from the heating elements that turn those liquids into a vapor.
In a study in _Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry_, researchers exposed mice to e-cigarette vapor twice a day over four days to better understand how metal builds up in a user's lungs.
The mice were divided into three groups, receiving the equivalent of eight, 16 or 32 vaping puffs in each session.
A fourth group only breathed normal air.
The device the researchers used to produce the vapor had a nickel-chromium heating element.
They used a commercially available vape liquid, which they analyzed and found also contained those two metals, as well as zinc, aluminum, copper, lead, mercury and more.
After four days of breathing the vapor, the researchers examined the mice's lungs, using a laser-based imaging system to map exactly where the metals had settled.
They found that different metals tended to build up in different places.
Lead and nickel settled more in the upper area of the lungs, as well as in the outer lining.
Zinc was found in higher concentrations at the bottom of the lungs.
There was evidence of metal in the lungs of all the mice that were exposed to the vapor.
For mice in the 32-puffs group, lead concentrations were 25 times higher than among the mice that just breathed normal air.
Many of the metals left by vaping are linked to health risks.
For example, nickel may damage the cells lining the airways.
And lead can be absorbed into the bloodstream, spreading to bones, the brain and other organs, where it may contribute to high blood pressure and cognitive problems.

articles.title: Sushi Named the Top Japanese Food to Share Overseas
articles.intro: This lesson explores a survey about Japanese foods people most want to share overseas, with sushi topping the list, followed by tempura and miso soup.

sentences.text: What do you think of when you hear "Japanese food"?
Sushi?
Ramen?
Tempura?
This is what 600 people in Japan were asked in a survey by Suzumo Machinery.
And eight in 10 people said they think of sushi, making it the top answer!
Tempura came second, named by 57% of people.
Miso soup was third, named by 44%.
Next were udon, soba and onigiri.
The survey also asked people in Japan what Japanese food they want people in other countries to taste.
Sushi was again the top answer, named by 68% of people.
Tempura came second, named by 42%.
_Shabu-shabu_ and _sukiyaki_ were next, followed by ramen and {{prn:_onigiri_|onigheeri}}.
But while miso soup was third on the list of food people in Japan think of, it was only eighth on the list of food they want people in other countries to taste.
Sushi is already very popular outside Japan, and there are many sushi restaurants in other countries.
So what's the most important thing when making sushi for people outside Japan?
Seventy percent of people said the taste and quality are the most important things — and 35% said taste and quality are important even if they make the sushi more expensive.
Just 16% said it's more important that the sushi is cheap.
The survey shows that Japanese people are happy to share their food with the world — but it has to taste right!

articles.title: 54% of Americans Use AI for Gift Ideas
articles.intro: Explore how over half of Americans are using AI for holiday gift ideas, comfort levels with AI shopping, and trends in gift preferences.

sentences.text: With Christmas on the way, many people are already thinking about what to buy their loved ones as gifts — and AI might be helping more Americans with their holiday shopping than they'd like to admit!
Visa's 2026 Holiday Spending Shift Survey asked 1,000 people in the US about their plans for holiday spending this year.
The survey was done in September of this year, when 54% of participants said they had already used AI in some way for shopping, up from 47% at the same time in 2025.
Nearly a quarter said they were more comfortable using AI for shopping this year compared with last year.
Sixty-one percent of participants said they were comfortable letting AI compare prices for them, while 59% said they felt OK using it to check product availability.
And 54% were comfortable asking AI to suggest gifts for people.
However, 41% said they wouldn't tell someone that they'd let AI help choose their gift!
Also, even if more Americans are happy to use AI to help them look for things, most still aren't sure about letting it do the actual purchasing.
According to Visa, only 23% of Americans trust AI to handle payments for them.
The survey also found out what's topping Americans' gift lists this year.
Sixty percent of survey participants said they'd be most excited to either give or receive travel experiences as a gift, while 55% said the same for tickets to a live event.
However, only 15% said they were prioritizing things like travel and events in what they were actually planning to buy for people, compared with 27% prioritizing physical items.

articles.title: Sit-Stand Desks Improve Productivity, Study Finds
articles.intro: This lesson explores research showing that sit-stand desks boost workplace productivity and offer health benefits compared to traditional desks.

sentences.text: When you think about a hardworking office, you might picture people sitting at desks for hours at a time.
But getting up off those chairs could be the key to getting more done!
Research has found that desks that let workers choose between sitting and standing are linked with higher levels of productivity.
A study published in _Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics_ looked at a year's worth of data from 10,000 office workers at a large US company.
The workers had either a normal desk that they just sat at, or one with an adjustable height that let them choose between sitting or standing when they liked.
To be part of the study, they had to have been using their desk for one year before it started, and could not change it during the research.
The researchers looked at data from software that tracked the participants' computer use.
They found that across the year, workers who used sit-stand desks used their computers an average of 43 minutes more each day compared to people who could only sit to work.
The researchers say this increased productivity could be worth almost an extra $9,000 per employee per year.
That extra activity was far more than just moving a mouse around too.
Workers at sit-stand desks generally typed more words and made more keystrokes, suggesting they were doing meaningful work.
Sit-stand desks may have important health benefits too.
Instead of having to spend too much time sitting or standing during the day, both of which can cause back and joint pain, sit-stand desks let workers change their position as they feel they need to.

articles.title: More Time in Light Could Reduce Dementia Risk
articles.intro: This lesson explores research on how increased daylight exposure may help reduce the risk of dementia and explains key related concepts.

sentences.text: Dementia is becoming a serious global health challenge.
In 2020, there were at least 55 million people around the world living with it.
But dementia mainly affects older people.
And as improvements in other areas of health lead to longer lifespans, the number of people with dementia is expected to rise to 78 million by 2030, and 139 million by 2050.
Dementia isn't one single disease either.
It can be caused by many different conditions — such as Alzheimer's disease — that are linked with an accumulation of waste proteins in the brain and a decline in cognitive function.
While there is no cure, research points to lifestyle interventions as having protective effects.
And one study has found that just spending time in the sun may support brain health and reduce the risk of developing dementia.
The study, published in _General Psychiatry_, included almost 88,000 participants with an average age of 62, and who were all dementia-free at the outset of the research.
They each wore a wrist device for seven days that measured their exposure to light during both the day and night.
After an average follow-up period of eight years, 741 participants had developed dementia.
And the researchers found that being exposed to an average daytime light level above 1,000 lux was linked with a 16% lower risk of dementia.
A lux is a standard unit to measure light, and is based on how much light falls on a surface.
One lux is about the same as how much a regular candle lights up one square meter around it — and 1,000 lux is the equivalent of light from the sun on a very overcast day.
Full sunlight can measure 100,000 lux or more.
And the study found that spending an average of at least 42 minutes in moderate daytime light of at least 5,000 lux was linked to a 17% reduced risk of dementia.
Meanwhile, spending less than 42 minutes in 5,000 lux light was a greater predictor of dementia than alcohol consumption, which is a well-established risk factor.

articles.intro: Explore recent research on the key factors that predict children's reading abilities, including cognitive and language skills.

sentences.text: Teachers know — and researchers have confirmed — that good literacy skills can really help a child when they're trying to learn a second language.
This is because the reading and writing skills they learn in their first language carry over into any new languages they learn.
And one study published in _Journal of Intelligence_ has now challenged some common beliefs about what makes a child a good reader.
According to the researchers at Texas A&M University, many people believe that smart kids just read well, while kids who aren't as smart don't.
And some children who have problems with reading must have issues with visual processing and how they see text.
However, the researchers looked at a wide range of cognitive and achievement tests to look at nearly 50,000 possible relationships between different types of cognitive abilities and reading results.
And they found that people's common beliefs about reading aren't really right.
The researchers did find that general intelligence matters to reading, but far less than older research suggested.
And, perhaps most surprisingly, visual processing showed no real relationship with reading skills.
Instead, auditory processing — being able to hear and decode the sounds in words — was found to have a far greater effect on reading skills.
Something known as "comprehension-knowledge" also turned out to be important for reading.
This refers to all the ideas, words and background knowledge children build up from the world around them.
In fact, these two skills were the greatest predictors of reading ability among children.
Memory, mental processing speed and reasoning also played important roles.
These findings could give both teachers and parents better ways to support children with reading.
"Strengthening foundational skills at home, even the ones that seem simple, can have meaningful effects on more advanced reading abilities," said researcher Daniel Hajovsky.

articles.title: Japan's School Costs Rise as Subsidies Not Enough
articles.intro: Explore how rising costs and limited subsidies are making it harder for families in Japan to afford private high school education.

sentences.text: In Japan, third-year junior high school students take extremely competitive exams to get into their chosen public or private high school.
And about one-third of high school students go to a private high school, which can actually be easier to get into than a public school — but more expensive.

This year, Japan introduced a subsidy system covering most tuition costs for private high schools, offering up to about {{prn:460,000|four hundred and sixty thousand}} yen, or around {{prn:$2,900|two thousand and nine hundred dollars}}, per student.
But while this made it easier for poorer families to access private schools, there are still a number of fees they wouldn't pay at public schools — and those fees are going up.
For example, in addition to tuition, private schools charge facility fees for things like heating, cooling and building maintenance.

And private high school facility fees this year were double those of 2025, rising from an average of {{prn:73,000|seventy three thousand}} yen — about {{prn:$460|four hundred and sixty dollars}} — to {{prn:147,000|one hundred and forty seven thousand}} yen, or about {{prn:$930|nine hundred and thirty dollars}}.
That's based on a survey by nongovernmental organization Save the Children Japan.

In May and June, it surveyed {{prn:125|one hundred and twenty five}} first-year junior and senior high school students and {{prn:425|four hundred and twenty five}} parents from financially struggling families across the country.

It also found that enrollment fees — which are separate from tuition fees, and not covered by the government subsidy — have gone up by nearly 20% to around {{prn:173,000|one hundred and seventy three thousand}} yen, or about {{prn:$1,100|one thousand and one hundred dollars}}.
The average cost of computers and tablets has also gone up by almost 10%.
And while 55% of public schools offer financial support to buy these devices, only 7% of private schools do.
Half of the parents with children in private schools said they were worried that their children might have to leave their school because of increasing costs.

articles.title: Cranberry Juice May Fight Tooth Decay — Study
articles.intro: This lesson examines a study on how pure cranberry juice may slow dental plaque growth and help prevent tooth decay.

sentences.text: Mostly grown in North America, cranberries are tart fruits that are high in vitamins and minerals.
They're considered a healthy snack — and one study now suggests that cranberry juice may even help protect against tooth decay.
The study, published in _Scientific Reports_,  found that pure cranberry juice could slow the growth of dental plaque, and reduce the production of acids that contribute to tooth decay.
Dental plaque is the sticky film of bacteria that regularly forms on teeth.
Having some plaque is normal, but too much can lead to cavities, infections, gum disease and tooth loss.
This is because, when we eat, the bacteria in plaque feed on sugars and produce acids that erode the teeth.
Cranberries are already used to fight some bacterial infections, because they contain chemicals that "unstick" bacteria from cells.
To see if they could also fight off the bacteria in plaque, researchers worked with eight adults and 14 children, who were all given one of three drinks.
One group was given 100% pure, unsweetened cranberry juice.
Another group had a drink that was 27% cranberry juice with added sugar.
The final group just got water.
On the morning of the experiment, participants arrived at the laboratory having not brushed their teeth after they woke up, so they'd have a night's worth of plaque buildup.
Researchers swabbed the teeth on one side of their mouths to get a sample of plaque.
After rinsing their mouths with water, the participants drank three small amounts of their assigned beverage, swishing each sip around their mouth several times.
After 30 minutes, researchers swabbed the other side of the participants' mouths — this time getting samples from the teeth not used in the first collection.
When they compared the sets of samples, the researchers found that plaque exposed to pure cranberry juice grew more slowly than plaque that was just exposed to water.
These samples also showed less acid production.
While the 27% cranberry drink had only an extremely small effect, the results still suggest that cranberries may benefit oral health.

articles.title: 1 in 4 South Korean High Schoolers Sleep Under 5 Hours
articles.intro: This lesson examines a report on South Korean high schoolers' sleep habits, highlighting the causes and effects of severe sleep deprivation.

sentences.text: Getting just five hours of sleep might be OK for a night or two.
But imagine sleeping that little almost every night.
For more than one in four high school students in South Korea, that's what a normal school week looks like.
A new report has found that 27% of high school students get less than five hours of sleep on weekdays, while six in ten get fewer than six hours.
The report, published by the National Youth Policy Institute, looked at survey answers from over 54,000 middle and high school students across the country.
Health experts recommend that teenagers aged 13 to 18 get eight to ten hours of sleep a night.
But in South Korea, just 4% of high school students get at least eight hours on weekdays.
And more than 70% don't even go to bed until after 1 a.m.
The report also found that students start losing sleep when they enter high school.
Average weekday sleep drops from 6.4 hours in the final year of middle school to 5.6 hours in the first year of high school — almost 50 minutes a night.
It's no surprise that many try to catch up on sleep on weekends.
Across all the students surveyed, average sleep time increased from 6.3 hours on weekdays to 8.2 hours on weekends.
And getting so little sleep may be affecting their mental health.
Among students who sleep less than five hours, 33% reported feeling depressed and 58% reported high stress levels — nearly twice as many among those sleeping eight hours or more.

articles.title: Venice Tops List of World's Quietest Cities
articles.intro: Explore how Venice was named the world’s quietest city and discover what makes other European cities peaceful travel destinations.

sentences.text: Going on vacation to a big city doesn't have to mean living with noise.
In fact, many cities can be very quiet.
Try Venice, Italy, for example, which has been named the world's quietest city on a list shared by Avanti Travel Insurance.
The company started by looking at Euromonitor's 2025 list of the 100 best city destinations.
It then measured a 2-kilometre radius from the center of each city and looked at how many big, noisy roads were in this area, and how long they were.

It also looked at how many of the streets in the area were for pedestrians only, and finalized the top 10 by seeing if they had rules that could make an area more peaceful, like limits on store opening times and on traffic at nearby airports.
Venice's famous canals helped push it to the top of the list: instead of cars and buses, people get around the city center by boat or on foot.
Many stores in Venice also close on Sundays, with some not opening on Monday mornings either.
It's also normal for food stores to close on Wednesday afternoons, giving the city center's already pedestrianized streets some very quiet hours.
Italy had two more cities in the top 10 after Venice, with Milan at number eight and Florence at number nine.
Every city in the top 10 was in Europe.
The second quietest city on the list was Lisbon, Portugal, which has few busy roads in its center and a limit on the number of night flights at its main airport.
This means a quiet night is less likely to be interrupted by a Boeing 737 flying overhead!
The third quietest city was Amsterdam in the Netherlands.
Like Venice, canals and car-free streets keep things quiet in this popular tourist destination.

articles.title: Can Playing Music Make Children Smarter?
articles.intro: This lesson explores whether learning a musical instrument can make children smarter, discussing recent research and its findings.

sentences.text: Listening to a child practice the drums might not be everyone's idea of a fun afternoon — but all that noise could come with some surprising benefits!
A new US study has found that children who play a musical instrument often do better on tests of intelligence, memory, reading and math.
Researchers from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign studied children aged 7 to 9.
They looked at 38 children who practiced an instrument for more than 30 minutes a week, and 38 children who didn't have musical training.
The results showed that children who played instruments did better on tests of intelligence and thinking skills.
They also scored higher on tests of working memory.
Working memory is what lets you hold information in your mind for a short time while using it to complete a task, such as remembering a phone number while typing it into your phone.
Children with musical training also did better in reading and math.
So does this mean that learning an instrument makes children smarter?
Well, not necessarily.
The researchers explained that the study couldn't prove that playing music caused the higher scores.
For example, children who learn instruments might also take part in other activities that help them learn.
Also, children who played instruments didn't do better on every test.
For example, in one test, children had to draw a line through a difficult path without lifting their pencil.
Both groups did about the same.
More research is needed to understand how music and learning are connected.
But the next time you hear a child practicing the drums, remember that all that noise might have some benefits!

articles.title: Record Number of People Injured by Nara Deer
articles.intro: Learn about Nara's sacred deer, rising tourist-related injuries, reasons for the increase, and advice for staying safe around these wild animals.

sentences.text: Japan's ancient city of Nara is popular with tourists for its many shrines, temples and gardens.
But Nara has something else that's rather unusual — a large park where deer and humans mix freely.
Deer have lived with humans in Nara for over {{prn:1,300|one thousand and three hundred}} years, so they're quite used to us!
The Nara deer are believed to be sacred messengers of the Shinto gods, so they're protected.
A common activity for tourists is feeding the deer special rice crackers called _shika senbei_, and the deer will approach people hoping for these treats.
However, it's important to remember that even though these deer are used to humans, they're still wild animals.
And sometimes the deer can be a little aggressive when people forget that they're wild.

In fact, according to Nara City Hospital, the number of people who have had to go to hospital after being injured by deer in Nara has been increasing over the last five years — and this year, it already reached a record high of 51 people by November 5.
The increase in injuries is said to be because of increases in the number of deer — and also increases in the number of visitors to Nara.

This year, the Nara Deer Preservation Foundation counted {{prn:1,687|one thousand six hundred and eighty seven}} deer in Nara — a record high, and an increase of {{prn:222|two hundred and twenty two}} from last year.
Experts warn that some tourists may have the wrong idea about the animals, thinking they're friendly and can be petted.
But people can be knocked over by the deer or hurt by their antlers.

The website of the Nara Deer Preservation Foundation suggests that people do not approach the deer or touch them, and if people have rice crackers for the deer, they should give them to the deer quickly and not tease the animals.
Elderly people and people with small children should be especially careful around the deer.

articles.title: Workplace Disputes Very Common in UK Companies
articles.intro: Explore the causes, costs, and rising trends of workplace disputes in UK companies, including bullying, harassment, and employer challenges.

sentences.text: Workplace disputes — serious disagreements between employees and their colleagues or with their employers — can take many forms.
Disagreements can arise over things like communication styles, how employees are treated, how workloads are shared, or over how much time an employee is absent from work.
And when disputes do arise, they can cost companies a lot in both time and money.
Now, a new survey has found that 93% of UK employers have experienced at least one workplace dispute in the last two years, with 63% resulting in attempted legal action.
Insurance firm Gallagher surveyed over 500 UK employers in September this year.

It found that, on average, workplace disputes cost employers more than $3,400 to resolve, and 59% of employers said that dealing with disputes had taken up at least 25 hours of company time over the past two years.
And disputes can also affect a company's reputation.
Sixty-eight percent of employers said that the company's reputation had been affected by a dispute.
This included 26% who experienced negative social media comments, 26% who were affected by negative online reviews and 24% who experienced further complaints from employees.
Employers also shared what types of disputes are increasing.

Forty percent said that there was an increase in disagreements over flexible working, 37% said there was an increase in disputes over bullying, harassment or discrimination, and 36% said there was an increase in sickness, absence or disability-related disputes.

And as for the reasons for the increases, thirty-three percent of employers said that disputes were becoming more common because of the changing expectations of employees, while 30% said it was because of hybrid or remote working.

Alistair Dornan, a managing director at Gallagher, said that to avoid workplace disagreements becoming costly and time-consuming disputes, employers needed clear policies, manager training, and early intervention.

"Investing in manager training is key to this, ensuring those on the front line have the confidence and skills to navigate difficult conversations, resolve issues early and prevent disputes becoming costly legal battles," said Dornan.

The company announced its new mascot in Tokyo on November 18.
The rabbit was chosen in a public vote.
People could choose from three characters: a squirrel, a rabbit, and a third character carrying a small mole in a bag.
JR East chose the three characters from designs made by young artists.
The company said it wanted a friendly new character that people could feel close to.
In total, around 1.6 million votes were cast, and the purple rabbit was the most popular choice, with about 860,000 votes.
But not everyone is happy about the change.
When JR East first announced that the penguin would be leaving, the news surprised many people.
And when the company showed the three possible new mascots in September, many people online said they didn't like the designs.
Some felt that none of the new characters was as good as the penguin.
The penguin has been part of Suica since 2001, and its picture can be seen on the cards.

articles.intro: Explore how Ichiran brings its unique ramen restaurant experience home with a miniature booth kit that recreates private dining and take-home noodles.

sentences.text: At most ramen restaurants in Japan, customers sit side by side, with little privacy as they eat their noodles.
But at the Ichiran restaurant chain, customers have their own private spaces to enjoy their meal.
Customers sit at a long counter, with partitions separating each seat.
Ramen is served through an opening in front of each customer, and it can be covered by a bamboo screen.
This way, customers can enjoy their meal without being disturbed by other people — even the staff.
Ichiran calls these seats "Flavor Concentration Booths."
Now, the chain has released a miniature version of its famous booths that people can set up on a table or desk at home.
The kit includes partitions and signs like those found at Ichiran restaurants.
It even has a working bamboo screen that can be moved up and down!
The home booth is small — it's only 33 centimeters high — but there's enough space to pass a bowl of ramen through the opening at the front.
At Ichiran restaurants, customers can use a button to call staff when they need help, or to order extra noodles if they still have soup left.
The home booth has its own button too, and it plays the same chime that you can hear in Ichiran restaurants.
Of course, you'll still have to prepare and serve the noodles yourself!
The Flavor Concentration Booth kit was released on November 4 as part of the 10th anniversary of Ichiran's take-home ramen, which first went on sale in 2016.

The kit comes with five servings of take-home ramen for {{prn:3,500|three thousand and five hundred}} yen — about {{prn:$22|twenty two dollars}} — or 10 servings for {{prn:4,527|four thousand five hundred and twenty seven}} yen, or about {{prn:$28|twenty eight dollars}}.

articles.title: Cats May Meow to Ask Us to Solve Their Problems
articles.intro: Explore research on why cats meow more around humans and how meowing might be their way of asking us for help with their problems.

sentences.text: Your cat has a problem — so, naturally, it's your problem too!
Maybe they're trying to tell you they're hungry, or that they want to play.
But they won't stop meowing until you solve the problem.
And a new study suggests that this meowing may really be a cat's way of asking for help.
It found that cats are more than four times as likely to meow when humans are around!
The study was done by researchers in Brazil, and included 38 pet cats.
The owners said their cats meowed a lot around food.
So each cat had their favorite treat put inside a small plastic box that had holes in it.
Although they could smell the treat, they could not open the box.
The researchers then observed the cats for one minute under two different conditions: alone, and with a person in the room.
The cats meowed 86 times when a human was in the room, compared with 20 meows when the cats were alone.
The researchers also noticed that, when a person was in the room, the cats looked at them a lot — sometimes looking from the person to the treat box.
When the cats were alone, they mostly stood still and looked at the door.
The results suggest that, when faced with a problem they couldn't solve, the cats were more likely to meow if a human was around to help.
However, the researchers said this study could not confirm that every meow was a deliberate request.
The study was also quite small, and was done with cats that were already known to meow around food.
But the next time you hear a cat meow, it might be trying to tell you something!

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin Hold Historic Talks in China
articles.intro: Explore the historic summit between Trump, Xi, and Putin in China, their joint declaration, and the political implications for global security and diplomacy.

sentences.text: US President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin have held their first-ever three-way summit, presenting themselves as partners in promoting peace but offering few concrete commitments.
The leaders met in Shenzhen, China, on November 19, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ({{prn:APEC|A-pack}}) summit.
Their talks lasted more than an hour.
The leaders emphasized their countries' roles as World War II victors and their shared responsibility for maintaining international security.
Their joint "peace declaration" called for reforms to the United Nations, increased oil supplies and dialogue to reduce nuclear risks.
However, it did not explain the type and extent of the UN reforms the leaders agreed to.
The statement also made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.
Trump described the gathering as "really making history" and presented it as a starting point for tackling international problems.
He said he and Xi agreed that Iran should fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies, and must not obtain a nuclear weapon.
However, there was no sign that he secured commitments from either Xi or Putin to help resolve the Iran conflict.
For Putin, the meeting offered an opportunity to present Russia as a global power equal to the US and China.
It was his first appearance at an APEC summit since 2017.
The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, and criticized the International Criminal Court (ICC).
Putin faces an ICC arrest warrant for alleged war crimes in Ukraine, while the US opposes its warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
For Xi, hosting the event reinforced China's growing diplomatic influence.
Beijing wanted to present itself as a power promoting peace while steering the meeting away from specifics, according to Ruby Osman, a policy adviser at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.
{{prn:Xi |shee}} expressed optimism about the potential for future cooperation.
"As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace," he said.

articles.title: How Your Morning Mood May Affect Your Workday
articles.intro: Explore how your mood in the morning can impact focus and productivity at work, based on a study of feelings, sleep, and workplace flow.

sentences.text: The alarm goes off, and it's time to get up for work.
On some mornings, we're ready to start the day.
On others, we just want to turn off the alarm and go back to sleep.
But could the way we feel about the day ahead affect how well we focus at work?
Well, a new study suggests that it could.
Researchers from Canada and Germany studied 102 people over two working weeks.
The participants answered questions three times a day, sharing how they felt before, during and after their working day.
The researchers wanted to understand something called "flow."
This is when we're so focused on what we're doing that we forget about everything else — and work very well.
They found that people who looked forward to their day were more likely to experience flow.
People who expected to learn new things or face challenges also seemed a little more likely to experience flow, but the results were less clear.
Those who were worried that the day would be difficult or stressful were less likely to experience flow.
The researchers also looked at sleep.
They found that people who slept better were more likely to look forward to the day ahead and less likely to worry about it.
And there was another interesting finding — people who experienced more flow during the day were less likely to lie in bed at night thinking about problems from their jobs.
The researchers said employers can help by giving their staff clear goals and time to focus without interruptions.
Of course, the study doesn't prove that positive thoughts lead to better days at work.
But it does suggest that the way we think about the day ahead may make a difference to how well we focus!

articles.title: Weekly Park Visits Help Kids Both Socially and Emotionally
articles.intro: This lesson explores a study on how weekly park visits support children's social and emotional development, with insights into family differences.

sentences.text: Taking children to a park at least once a week can help both their social and emotional development, according to a new study from the University of Exeter in the UK.
The study used data from over 4,000 children who took part in the UK's Children of the 90s study, which has followed children's development from the early 1990s to the present day.
Data on problems with the children's behavior, emotions and ability to form relationships with others was collected in surveys at five points between the ages of 4 and 11.

Looking at the data, the researchers found that children who were taken to the park at least once a week at every age had fewer social, emotional and behavioral problems than those who went less than once a week.
For children who went to parks more at some ages and less at others, it was also found that they had fewer problems during the times when they went to parks more.
The researchers said parks may help children's social and emotional development by giving them chances to enjoy physical activity, play with other children, and have time with their parents.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, children generally went to parks more when they were younger, and less as they got older.
But at young ages, children from richer families were taken to parks more often than children from poorer families.
Then, as they got older, children from poorer families started to go to parks a little more often than those in richer families.
The researchers suggest that this may be because richer parents are better able to take time off work and go to parks together when their children are younger.
And while richer parents can pay for other activities as their children get older, poorer families continue to use parks longer because they're free.

articles.title: Just 28% of Japanese Parents Want a Second Child
articles.intro: This lesson explores why fewer Japanese parents want a second child, highlighting financial pressures and changing attitudes toward family size.

sentences.text: Japan's population has been getting smaller and smaller for years.
The government wants people to have more children — but while some are happy to have one child, it might be more difficult to convince them to have a second!
Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance did a survey with {{prn:1,100|one thousand and one hundred}} parents who have one child aged between 0 and 6.
And just 28% said they would like to have another child — down from 57% in 2020.
Prices have been increasing in Japan and other parts of the world for some time, and this has put pressure on families that already have children.
In fact, the top reason given when parents were asked what's stopping them from having more children was worries about having enough money in the future.
The next biggest reason parents gave for not having another child was their age.
Around eight in 10 parents said they were feeling the impact of higher prices on their family spending.
Parents are finding it especially hard to keep up with the costs of food and extracurricular activities.
When asked what would make them think about having a second child, many said an increase in their income or their partner's income would make them more likely to have another child.

The survey also found that the average monthly cost of raising one child is {{prn:43,356|forty three thousand three hundred and fifty six}} yen — about {{prn:$270 — in 2026|two hundred and seventy dollars in twenty twenty six}} , up 5% from last year.
In 2018, when the survey began, the average monthly cost was {{prn:39,240|thirty nine thousand two hundred and forty}} yen, or about {{prn:$245|two hundred and forty five dollars}}.

articles.title: More than Half of People in Japan Use AI
articles.intro: Explore how generative AI use has grown across different age groups in Japan, popular AI tools, and common uses based on recent survey data.

sentences.text: From answering questions to writing emails and helping with everyday tasks, generative AI is becoming part of day-to-day life for more people in Japan.
A new survey by the Nippon Research Center found that 56% of people aged 20 to 69 had used generative AI as of June 2026.
And for the first time, just over half of those who were surveyed said they were currently using the technology.
And it's not just young people who are using AI more.
People in their 20s were still the most likely to have tried it, at 68%, followed by those in their 30s at 61% and those in their 40s at 58%.
But older generations are catching up.
Among people in their 50s, 55% had used generative AI, while 45% of those in their 60s had tried it.
In March 2025, both groups were still at around 20%.
So which AI tools are people in Japan using?
ChatGPT was the most popular, with 30% of people saying they currently use it.
Google's Gemini was close behind at 29%, followed by Microsoft's Copilot at 15%.
The survey also looked at what people were using these tools for.
Finding information and doing research was the most common reason, mentioned by around 60% of current AI users.
Another 30% used AI to come up with ideas, while about a quarter used it to write or check emails and documents.
Interestingly, the share of people using AI for research has been growing, while the share using it to generate ideas has fallen.

articles.title: Tokyo's Akihabara Gets Solar-Powered Trash Cans
articles.intro: This lesson explores how Tokyo's Akihabara is using solar-powered, smart trash cans to address street waste with innovative technology.

sentences.text: Tourists love visiting Japan for its history, food and more.
But there's one thing many tourists don't love: there aren't many trash cans!
This isn't just a problem for tourists.
In the last few years, popular neighborhoods in Tokyo and other cities have seen an increase in trash on the streets.
However, it's not as easy as just putting a few trash cans on the corner.
Local governments have found that these trash cans quickly overflow as they're used by both people on the street and people in nearby homes, and it can be expensive to keep emptying them.
One solution is to make trash cans that don't fill up so quickly.
And one neighborhood in Tokyo is trying a high-tech solution.
Akihabara, known as one of the best places in Tokyo for technology, has put 22 solar-powered SmaGo trash cans in 10 places around the area.
These trash cans can hold much more trash than normal ones, because they can compact the trash to a fifth of its size.
They also have an online system that lets workers check how full each can is, so they know when it needs to be emptied.
The trash cans come from a Tokyo tech company called Forcetec.
Akihabara isn't the first place to get SmaGo trash cans.
They're already found in other parts of Tokyo, as well as neighborhoods in Osaka, Kyoto and other prefectures.
But it's the first time a local government in Japan has put so many of these trash cans in one place.
And Akihabara hopes they'll help keep the neighborhood clean!

articles.title: UK Job Satisfaction Is at an All-Time Low
articles.intro: This lesson explores the decline in job satisfaction in the UK, reasons behind it, and its impact on employees and employers.

sentences.text: Most of us spend a large part of our lives at work, so it's important to feel happy with what we do!
But according to analysis from London's Resolution Foundation, many people in the UK are not satisfied with their jobs.
In fact, job satisfaction is at an all-time low.
The analysis is based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, which had over {{prn:4,600|four thousand and six hundred}} participants.
The survey results were published on November 3 this year.
The data showed that just 74% of British workers are satisfied with their jobs.
This is the lowest percentage since the question was first asked in 1989.
When asked if they have an interesting job, just 63% said yes — a decrease of 11 percentage points from 10 years ago.
There are several reasons why people may be feeling less satisfied with their jobs.
Many workers feel their salaries aren't good, especially with rising costs in the UK and other parts of the world.
Others are unhappy with their working hours — 61% say they want more flexibility, up from 46% 10 years ago.
People are also less willing to do extra work for their employers.
Ten years ago, 69% of workers said they were happy to work harder to help their company.
Now it's just 55%.
According to the Resolution Foundation, this decrease in job satisfaction is bad news for both employees and employers.
And John Curtice, who worked on the British Social Attitudes survey, said employers may need to offer better pay and more flexible working hours to keep employees happy and motivated.

articles.title: Cyclists in Japan Receive 16,000 'Blue Tickets' in 6 Months
articles.intro: This lesson covers Japan's new blue ticket system for cycling violations, common offenses, fines, city data, and its impact on accident rates.

sentences.text: Police in Japan have recorded nearly 16,000 bicycle traffic violations since April, according to data from the country's National Police Agency (NPA).
On April 1 of this year, the NPA started using a new "blue ticket" system, which lets police quickly fine cyclists for breaking traffic rules.
In the system's first six months, using a smartphone while riding was the most common violation, making up 43% of all tickets.
Those caught riding while using a phone receive a fine of {{prn:12,000|twelve thousand}} yen, or about {{prn:$76|seventy six dollars}}.
The second most common violation was failing to stop when required, followed by riding through a red light.
Other common violations included entering a railroad crossing when the gate was down, and riding on the wrong side of the road.
These violations all carry fines of between {{prn:3,000|three thousand}} yen and {{prn:7,000|seven thousand}} yen — or between about {{prn:$19|nineteen dollars}} and {{prn:$44|forty four dollars}}.
The rules must be followed by all cyclists aged 16 and over.
Tokyo had the highest number of tickets, with nearly {{prn:3,000,|three thousand}} followed by Osaka with close to {{prn:2,900|two thousand and nine hundred}}.
Saitama recorded almost {{prn:1,900|one thousand and nine hundred}} violations, while Aichi had over {{prn:1,700|one thousand and seven hundred}}.
The NPA also said that bicycle accidents decreased by about 9% between April and September compared with the same time last year.
However, it said it's not clear if this is because of the new ticket system.
